canonical

kuh-NON-ih-kul -- shares a root with 'canon,' meaning an accepted set of rules or works. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Canonical is conforming to a general or accepted rule or principle.

Scholars still debate which manuscript represents the canonical version of the ancient poem.

Worked Example

Programmers argue for years about the 'right' way to format their code, until the community finally settles on one accepted style that every new textbook teaches from then on.

That officially accepted, standard version everyone agrees to follow is exactly what canonical describes. Unlike 'alternative,' which suggests just one option among many, canonical names the version a whole community has settled on and now measures other work against.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

official: Official means formally approved or issued by the organization or authority in charge -- an official schedule comes stamped from the office that runs things. Canonical status can grow instead from a community of scholars or readers gradually accepting one version as the standard, with no office issuing anything.

authoritative: Authoritative describes a source you trust because of who stands behind it -- a recognized expert or a body with the power to decide. Canonical describes the version itself: the one a field has accepted as its standard, however that acceptance came about.

established: Established means securely in place because it has been around long enough to feel settled -- an established routine or an established firm. Canonical is a stronger, more formal claim: not merely long-standing, but recognized as the accepted standard version that other work is measured against.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unofficial: not formally approved or recognized

apocryphal: of doubtful authenticity, though widely circulated

Where it sits · how officially accepted the version is — standard → canonical → definitive

standard vs. canonical: Standard is a more everyday word than canonical -- standard just means typical or usual, while canonical specifically implies a version has been formally accepted as the correct or official one.

definitive vs. canonical: Definitive goes a step beyond canonical -- a canonical version has been accepted by a community as the correct one, while a definitive version settles the question for good, leaving nothing left to argue.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — -canon-

root — -canon-: rule, standard (Greek (kanon))

suffix — -ical

suffix — -ical: relating to (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Greek kanon was a straight measuring rod, which came to mean 'a rule,' and -ical means 'relating to' -- so canonical describes whatever conforms to the accepted rule or principle. The same root gives us canon.

Use the root in a new word: canon

Use the root in a new word: canon: Fans have debated for years over which stories count as part of the series' official canon.
